"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both. "And what their hands made": the majority recited it with a hā'; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa recited "ʿamilat" without the hā'. "Mā" may be read in three ways:

The first: negation, meaning "and their hands did not make it"; that is, they found it made, and they had no hand in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil.

The second: the masdar sense, meaning "and from the work of their hands."

The third: the sense of "that which" (alladhī), [meaning "and that which their hands made"] of the tilling, planting, and grafting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. "Will they not give thanks" for His blessings?

"Glory be to Him who created the pairs" — the kinds and types — "all of them, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know. And a sign for them is the night: We strip off (naslakh) from it the day," that is, We remove and extract the day from it. Al-Kalbī said: "We take it away," "and behold, they are in darkness," that is, entering into the dark.

"And the sun runs on to a resting place for it," meaning toward its stationary point. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It does not reach its resting place until it returns to its stations. Qatādah said: until a fixed time for it that it does not exceed. It was said: until the end of its affair at the ending of the world. It was said: to its furthest setting-point.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Ibrāhīm ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bakkār al-ʿĪsī narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, saying: Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne." [75] [[Musnad Aḥmad: 5/158.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. The messengers here are the envoys of Jesus. The scholars of the reports about the prophets said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent two envoys from among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) to Antioch (Anṭākiya). When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending a few sheep, and he was Ḥabīb, the companion of Yā-Sīn. They greeted him, and the old man said: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus, calling you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes, we heal the sick and we cure the blind from birth and the leper, by God's permission." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill and bedridden for years." They said: "Then take us to your house, so we may see his condition."

He brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and at that moment he stood up healthy by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God healed many of the sick through their hands. The people had a king called Sallāḥīn.

He said: His name was Abṭayḥīs, one of the kings of the Romans, who worshipped idols. They said: The news reached him and he summoned them. He said to them: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "We cure the blind from birth and the leper, and we heal the sick, by God's permission." He said: "And for what did you come?" They said: "We came to call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees." The king said: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "Wait until I consider your matter." So the people followed them, seized them, and beat them in the marketplace.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent these two envoys to Antioch. They arrived there but did not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they glorified God and remembered Him. The king became angry, ordered them seized and imprisoned, and each of them was given one hundred lashes. They said: When the two envoys were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the head of the disciples, Shim'ūn al-Ṣafā (Simon Peter), after them to support them.

Shim'ūn entered the city disguised and began to associate with the king's retinue until they grew fond of him. His news was raised to the king, who summoned him, was pleased with his company, grew fond of him, and honored him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to other than your religion. Did you speak with them and hear their words?"

The king said: "Anger prevented me from that." He said: "Then, if the king sees fit, let him summon them so we may find out what they have."

The king summoned them, and Shim'ūn said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'ūn said: "Then describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and judges what He desires." Shim'ūn said: "And what is your sign?" They said to him: "Ask whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes were effaced, the place of his eyes like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight was split open. Then they took two balls of clay and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs, and he saw with them. The king marveled, and Shim'ūn said to the king: "Have you seen? If you asked your god to do the like of this, there would be honor for you and for your god."

The king said to him: "There is no secret with me. Our god that we worship neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Whenever the king entered the idol's place, Shim'ūn would enter with him, pray much, and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed.

The king said to the two envoys: "If your god whom you worship has power to revive the dead, we will believe in Him and in you." They said: "Our God is powerful over everything." The king said: "Here there is a dead man, the son of a landowner (dihqān), who died seven days ago. I have delayed burying him until his father returns, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, who had changed and begun to smell. They called upon their Lord openly, and Shim'ūn called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I died seven days ago, and I found a polytheist, so I was put into nine valleys of Fire. I warn you of what you are in; so believe in God."

Then he said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I looked and saw a youth of fair face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'ūn and these two," and he pointed to his two companions. The king marveled. When Shim'ūn knew that his word had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and invited him, and a group believed, and the king was among those who believed, while others disbelieved.

Ibn Isḥāq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people agreed to kill the envoys. This reached Ḥabīb, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the envoys. This is His saying, glorified is He: "When We sent to them two." 

They differed about their names. Ibn 'Abbās said: Tārūṣ and Mārūṣ. Wahb said: Yaḥyā and Yūnus. Muqātil said: Tūmān and Mānūṣ.

"But they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third." That is, We strengthened them with a third envoy. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and 'Āṣim, according to Ḥafṣ, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light pronunciation (fa-ʿazaznā, i.e., "so We overpowered"), from ʿazīz (mighty), meaning: "so We overpowered them," with a third envoy, who was Shim'ūn.

Muqātil said: Shim'ān. Ka'b said: The two envoys were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq, and the third was Shalūm. He attributed the sending to Himself because Jesus (peace be upon him) sent them only by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, and they were among the envoys. They all said to the people of Antioch: "Indeed, we are sent to you." They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying." That is, you are only liars. They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you. And our duty is only the clear conveyance." They said: "Indeed, we consider you an omen."

"[Your] omen is with you." Muqātil said: rain was withheld from them, and they said: "This is because of your ill omen." "If you do not desist, we will surely stone you." Qatādah said: with stones. Others said: we will kill you. "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us." They said: "Your omen is with you": your ill omen is with you because of your disbelief. Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: your share of good and evil.

Qatādah said: your deeds. And al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj recited "ṭayrukum" (your bird).

"Even if you are reminded?" That is, admonished. Abū Ja'far recited it with light pronunciation, meaning: because you were reminded. Its answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "Even if you are reminded, you say this?" "Rather, you are a people who are transgressing": polytheists exceeding the limit.

His saying: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city." He was Ḥabīb ibn Maryam. Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil said: Ḥabīb ibn Isrā'īl the carpenter (al-Najjār). Wahb said: He was a sickly man whose leprosy had spread, and his house was at the farthest gate of the city. He was a believer and charitable; he gathered his earnings in the evening and divided them into two halves: he fed his family one half and gave the other half in charity. When it reached him that his people intended to kill the envoys, he came to them and said:

"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both. "And what their hands made": the majority recited it with a hā'; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa recited "ʿamilat" without the hā'. "Mā" may be read in three ways:

The first: negation, meaning "and their hands did not make it"; that is, they found it made, and they had no hand in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil.

The second: the masdar sense, meaning "and from the work of their hands."

The third: the sense of "that which" (alladhī), [meaning "and that which their hands made"] of the tilling, planting, and grafting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. "Will they not give thanks" for His blessings?

"Glory be to Him who created the pairs" — the kinds and types — "all of them, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know. And a sign for them is the night: We strip off (naslakh) from it the day," that is, We remove and extract the day from it. Al-Kalbī said: "We take it away," "and behold, they are in darkness," that is, entering into the dark.

"And the sun runs on to a resting place for it," meaning toward its stationary point. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It does not reach its resting place until it returns to its stations. Qatādah said: until a fixed time for it that it does not exceed. It was said: until the end of its affair at the ending of the world. It was said: to its furthest setting-point.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Ibrāhīm ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bakkār al-ʿĪsī narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, saying: Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne." [75] [[Musnad Aḥmad: 5/158.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. The messengers here are the envoys of Jesus. The scholars of the reports about the prophets said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent two envoys from among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) to Antioch (Anṭākiya). When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending a few sheep, and he was Ḥabīb, the companion of Yā-Sīn. They greeted him, and the old man said: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus, calling you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes, we heal the sick and we cure the blind from birth and the leper, by God's permission." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill and bedridden for years." They said: "Then take us to your house, so we may see his condition."

He brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and at that moment he stood up healthy by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God healed many of the sick through their hands. The people had a king called Sallāḥīn.

He said: His name was Abṭayḥīs, one of the kings of the Romans, who worshipped idols. They said: The news reached him and he summoned them. He said to them: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "We cure the blind from birth and the leper, and we heal the sick, by God's permission." He said: "And for what did you come?" They said: "We came to call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees." The king said: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "Wait until I consider your matter." So the people followed them, seized them, and beat them in the marketplace.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent these two envoys to Antioch. They arrived there but did not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they glorified God and remembered Him. The king became angry, ordered them seized and imprisoned, and each of them was given one hundred lashes. They said: When the two envoys were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the head of the disciples, Shim'ūn al-Ṣafā (Simon Peter), after them to support them.

Shim'ūn entered the city disguised and began to associate with the king's retinue until they grew fond of him. His news was raised to the king, who summoned him, was pleased with his company, grew fond of him, and honored him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to other than your religion. Did you speak with them and hear their words?"

The king said: "Anger prevented me from that." He said: "Then, if the king sees fit, let him summon them so we may find out what they have."

The king summoned them, and Shim'ūn said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'ūn said: "Then describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and judges what He desires." Shim'ūn said: "And what is your sign?" They said to him: "Ask whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes were effaced, the place of his eyes like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight was split open. Then they took two balls of clay and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs, and he saw with them. The king marveled, and Shim'ūn said to the king: "Have you seen? If you asked your god to do the like of this, there would be honor for you and for your god."

The king said to him: "There is no secret with me. Our god that we worship neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Whenever the king entered the idol's place, Shim'ūn would enter with him, pray much, and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed.

The king said to the two envoys: "If your god whom you worship has power to revive the dead, we will believe in Him and in you." They said: "Our God is powerful over everything." The king said: "Here there is a dead man, the son of a landowner (dihqān), who died seven days ago. I have delayed burying him until his father returns, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, who had changed and begun to smell. They called upon their Lord openly, and Shim'ūn called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I died seven days ago, and I found a polytheist, so I was put into nine valleys of Fire. I warn you of what you are in; so believe in God."

Then he said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I looked and saw a youth of fair face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'ūn and these two," and he pointed to his two companions. The king marveled. When Shim'ūn knew that his word had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and invited him, and a group believed, and the king was among those who believed, while others disbelieved.

Ibn Isḥāq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people agreed to kill the envoys. This reached Ḥabīb, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the envoys. This is His saying, glorified is He: "When We sent to them two." 

They differed about their names. Ibn 'Abbās said: Tārūṣ and Mārūṣ. Wahb said: Yaḥyā and Yūnus. Muqātil said: Tūmān and Mānūṣ.

"But they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third." That is, We strengthened them with a third envoy. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and 'Āṣim, according to Ḥafṣ, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light pronunciation (fa-ʿazaznā, i.e., "so We overpowered"), from ʿazīz (mighty), meaning: "so We overpowered them," with a third envoy, who was Shim'ūn.

Muqātil said: Shim'ān. Ka'b said: The two envoys were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq, and the third was Shalūm. He attributed the sending to Himself because Jesus (peace be upon him) sent them only by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, and they were among the envoys. They all said to the people of Antioch: "Indeed, we are sent to you." They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying." That is, you are only liars. They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you. And our duty is only the clear conveyance." They said: "Indeed, we consider you an omen."

"[Your] omen is with you." Muqātil said: rain was withheld from them, and they said: "This is because of your ill omen." "If you do not desist, we will surely stone you." Qatādah said: with stones. Others said: we will kill you. "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us." They said: "Your omen is with you": your ill omen is with you because of your disbelief. Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: your share of good and evil.

Qatādah said: your deeds. And al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj recited "ṭayrukum" (your bird).

"Even if you are reminded?" That is, admonished. Abū Ja'far recited it with light pronunciation, meaning: because you were reminded. Its answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "Even if you are reminded, you say this?" "Rather, you are a people who are transgressing": polytheists exceeding the limit.

His saying: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city." He was Ḥabīb ibn Maryam. Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil said: Ḥabīb ibn Isrā'īl the carpenter (al-Najjār). Wahb said: He was a sickly man whose leprosy had spread, and his house was at the farthest gate of the city. He was a believer and charitable; he gathered his earnings in the evening and divided them into two halves: he fed his family one half and gave the other half in charity. When it reached him that his people intended to kill the envoys, he came to them and said:

"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both. "And what their hands made": the majority recited it with a hā'; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa recited "ʿamilat" without the hā'. "Mā" may be read in three ways:

The first: negation, meaning "and their hands did not make it"; that is, they found it made, and they had no hand in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil.

The second: the masdar sense, meaning "and from the work of their hands."

The third: the sense of "that which" (alladhī), [meaning "and that which their hands made"] of the tilling, planting, and grafting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. "Will they not give thanks" for His blessings?

"Glory be to Him who created the pairs" — the kinds and types — "all of them, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know. And a sign for them is the night: We strip off (naslakh) from it the day," that is, We remove and extract the day from it. Al-Kalbī said: "We take it away," "and behold, they are in darkness," that is, entering into the dark.

"And the sun runs on to a resting place for it," meaning toward its stationary point. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It does not reach its resting place until it returns to its stations. Qatādah said: until a fixed time for it that it does not exceed. It was said: until the end of its affair at the ending of the world. It was said: to its furthest setting-point.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Ibrāhīm ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bakkār al-ʿĪsī narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, saying: Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne." [75] [[Musnad Aḥmad: 5/158.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. The messengers here are the envoys of Jesus. The scholars of the reports about the prophets said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent two envoys from among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) to Antioch (Anṭākiya). When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending a few sheep, and he was Ḥabīb, the companion of Yā-Sīn. They greeted him, and the old man said: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus, calling you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes, we heal the sick and we cure the blind from birth and the leper, by God's permission." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill and bedridden for years." They said: "Then take us to your house, so we may see his condition."

He brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and at that moment he stood up healthy by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God healed many of the sick through their hands. The people had a king called Sallāḥīn.

He said: His name was Abṭayḥīs, one of the kings of the Romans, who worshipped idols. They said: The news reached him and he summoned them. He said to them: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "We cure the blind from birth and the leper, and we heal the sick, by God's permission." He said: "And for what did you come?" They said: "We came to call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees." The king said: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "Wait until I consider your matter." So the people followed them, seized them, and beat them in the marketplace.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent these two envoys to Antioch. They arrived there but did not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they glorified God and remembered Him. The king became angry, ordered them seized and imprisoned, and each of them was given one hundred lashes. They said: When the two envoys were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the head of the disciples, Shim'ūn al-Ṣafā (Simon Peter), after them to support them.

Shim'ūn entered the city disguised and began to associate with the king's retinue until they grew fond of him. His news was raised to the king, who summoned him, was pleased with his company, grew fond of him, and honored him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to other than your religion. Did you speak with them and hear their words?"

The king said: "Anger prevented me from that." He said: "Then, if the king sees fit, let him summon them so we may find out what they have."

The king summoned them, and Shim'ūn said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'ūn said: "Then describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and judges what He desires." Shim'ūn said: "And what is your sign?" They said to him: "Ask whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes were effaced, the place of his eyes like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight was split open. Then they took two balls of clay and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs, and he saw with them. The king marveled, and Shim'ūn said to the king: "Have you seen? If you asked your god to do the like of this, there would be honor for you and for your god."

The king said to him: "There is no secret with me. Our god that we worship neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Whenever the king entered the idol's place, Shim'ūn would enter with him, pray much, and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed.

The king said to the two envoys: "If your god whom you worship has power to revive the dead, we will believe in Him and in you." They said: "Our God is powerful over everything." The king said: "Here there is a dead man, the son of a landowner (dihqān), who died seven days ago. I have delayed burying him until his father returns, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, who had changed and begun to smell. They called upon their Lord openly, and Shim'ūn called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I died seven days ago, and I found a polytheist, so I was put into nine valleys of Fire. I warn you of what you are in; so believe in God."

Then he said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I looked and saw a youth of fair face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'ūn and these two," and he pointed to his two companions. The king marveled. When Shim'ūn knew that his word had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and invited him, and a group believed, and the king was among those who believed, while others disbelieved.

Ibn Isḥāq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people agreed to kill the envoys. This reached Ḥabīb, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the envoys. This is His saying, glorified is He: "When We sent to them two." 

They differed about their names. Ibn 'Abbās said: Tārūṣ and Mārūṣ. Wahb said: Yaḥyā and Yūnus. Muqātil said: Tūmān and Mānūṣ.

"But they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third." That is, We strengthened them with a third envoy. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and 'Āṣim, according to Ḥafṣ, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light pronunciation (fa-ʿazaznā, i.e., "so We overpowered"), from ʿazīz (mighty), meaning: "so We overpowered them," with a third envoy, who was Shim'ūn.

Muqātil said: Shim'ān. Ka'b said: The two envoys were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq, and the third was Shalūm. He attributed the sending to Himself because Jesus (peace be upon him) sent them only by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, and they were among the envoys. They all said to the people of Antioch: "Indeed, we are sent to you." They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying." That is, you are only liars. They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you. And our duty is only the clear conveyance." They said: "Indeed, we consider you an omen."

"[Your] omen is with you." Muqātil said: rain was withheld from them, and they said: "This is because of your ill omen." "If you do not desist, we will surely stone you." Qatādah said: with stones. Others said: we will kill you. "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us." They said: "Your omen is with you": your ill omen is with you because of your disbelief. Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: your share of good and evil.

Qatādah said: your deeds. And al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj recited "ṭayrukum" (your bird).

"Even if you are reminded?" That is, admonished. Abū Ja'far recited it with light pronunciation, meaning: because you were reminded. Its answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "Even if you are reminded, you say this?" "Rather, you are a people who are transgressing": polytheists exceeding the limit.

His saying: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city." He was Ḥabīb ibn Maryam. Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil said: Ḥabīb ibn Isrā'īl the carpenter (al-Najjār). Wahb said: He was a sickly man whose leprosy had spread, and his house was at the farthest gate of the city. He was a believer and charitable; he gathered his earnings in the evening and divided them into two halves: he fed his family one half and gave the other half in charity. When it reached him that his people intended to kill the envoys, he came to them and said:

"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both. "And what their hands made": the majority recited it with a hā'; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa recited "ʿamilat" without the hā'. "Mā" may be read in three ways:

The first: negation, meaning "and their hands did not make it"; that is, they found it made, and they had no hand in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil.

The second: the masdar sense, meaning "and from the work of their hands."

The third: the sense of "that which" (alladhī), [meaning "and that which their hands made"] of the tilling, planting, and grafting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. "Will they not give thanks" for His blessings?

"Glory be to Him who created the pairs" — the kinds and types — "all of them, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know. And a sign for them is the night: We strip off (naslakh) from it the day," that is, We remove and extract the day from it. Al-Kalbī said: "We take it away," "and behold, they are in darkness," that is, entering into the dark.

"And the sun runs on to a resting place for it," meaning toward its stationary point. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It does not reach its resting place until it returns to its stations. Qatādah said: until a fixed time for it that it does not exceed. It was said: until the end of its affair at the ending of the world. It was said: to its furthest setting-point.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Ibrāhīm ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bakkār al-ʿĪsī narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, saying: Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne." [75] [[Musnad Aḥmad: 5/158.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. The messengers here are the envoys of Jesus. The scholars of the reports about the prophets said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent two envoys from among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) to Antioch (Anṭākiya). When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending a few sheep, and he was Ḥabīb, the companion of Yā-Sīn. They greeted him, and the old man said: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus, calling you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes, we heal the sick and we cure the blind from birth and the leper, by God's permission." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill and bedridden for years." They said: "Then take us to your house, so we may see his condition."

He brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and at that moment he stood up healthy by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God healed many of the sick through their hands. The people had a king called Sallāḥīn.

He said: His name was Abṭayḥīs, one of the kings of the Romans, who worshipped idols. They said: The news reached him and he summoned them. He said to them: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "We cure the blind from birth and the leper, and we heal the sick, by God's permission." He said: "And for what did you come?" They said: "We came to call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees." The king said: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "Wait until I consider your matter." So the people followed them, seized them, and beat them in the marketplace.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent these two envoys to Antioch. They arrived there but did not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they glorified God and remembered Him. The king became angry, ordered them seized and imprisoned, and each of them was given one hundred lashes. They said: When the two envoys were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the head of the disciples, Shim'ūn al-Ṣafā (Simon Peter), after them to support them.

Shim'ūn entered the city disguised and began to associate with the king's retinue until they grew fond of him. His news was raised to the king, who summoned him, was pleased with his company, grew fond of him, and honored him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to other than your religion. Did you speak with them and hear their words?"

The king said: "Anger prevented me from that." He said: "Then, if the king sees fit, let him summon them so we may find out what they have."

The king summoned them, and Shim'ūn said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'ūn said: "Then describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and judges what He desires." Shim'ūn said: "And what is your sign?" They said to him: "Ask whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes were effaced, the place of his eyes like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight was split open. Then they took two balls of clay and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs, and he saw with them. The king marveled, and Shim'ūn said to the king: "Have you seen? If you asked your god to do the like of this, there would be honor for you and for your god."

The king said to him: "There is no secret with me. Our god that we worship neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Whenever the king entered the idol's place, Shim'ūn would enter with him, pray much, and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed.

The king said to the two envoys: "If your god whom you worship has power to revive the dead, we will believe in Him and in you." They said: "Our God is powerful over everything." The king said: "Here there is a dead man, the son of a landowner (dihqān), who died seven days ago. I have delayed burying him until his father returns, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, who had changed and begun to smell. They called upon their Lord openly, and Shim'ūn called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I died seven days ago, and I found a polytheist, so I was put into nine valleys of Fire. I warn you of what you are in; so believe in God."

Then he said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I looked and saw a youth of fair face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'ūn and these two," and he pointed to his two companions. The king marveled. When Shim'ūn knew that his word had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and invited him, and a group believed, and the king was among those who believed, while others disbelieved.

Ibn Isḥāq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people agreed to kill the envoys. This reached Ḥabīb, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the envoys. This is His saying, glorified is He: "When We sent to them two." 

They differed about their names. Ibn 'Abbās said: Tārūṣ and Mārūṣ. Wahb said: Yaḥyā and Yūnus. Muqātil said: Tūmān and Mānūṣ.

"But they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third." That is, We strengthened them with a third envoy. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and 'Āṣim, according to Ḥafṣ, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light pronunciation (fa-ʿazaznā, i.e., "so We overpowered"), from ʿazīz (mighty), meaning: "so We overpowered them," with a third envoy, who was Shim'ūn.

Muqātil said: Shim'ān. Ka'b said: The two envoys were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq, and the third was Shalūm. He attributed the sending to Himself because Jesus (peace be upon him) sent them only by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, and they were among the envoys. They all said to the people of Antioch: "Indeed, we are sent to you." They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying." That is, you are only liars. They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you. And our duty is only the clear conveyance." They said: "Indeed, we consider you an omen."

"[Your] omen is with you." Muqātil said: rain was withheld from them, and they said: "This is because of your ill omen." "If you do not desist, we will surely stone you." Qatādah said: with stones. Others said: we will kill you. "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us." They said: "Your omen is with you": your ill omen is with you because of your disbelief. Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: your share of good and evil.

Qatādah said: your deeds. And al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj recited "ṭayrukum" (your bird).

"Even if you are reminded?" That is, admonished. Abū Ja'far recited it with light pronunciation, meaning: because you were reminded. Its answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "Even if you are reminded, you say this?" "Rather, you are a people who are transgressing": polytheists exceeding the limit.

His saying: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city." He was Ḥabīb ibn Maryam. Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil said: Ḥabīb ibn Isrā'īl the carpenter (al-Najjār). Wahb said: He was a sickly man whose leprosy had spread, and his house was at the farthest gate of the city. He was a believer and charitable; he gathered his earnings in the evening and divided them into two halves: he fed his family one half and gave the other half in charity. When it reached him that his people intended to kill the envoys, he came to them and said:

"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both.
