Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. The messengers here are the envoys of Jesus. The scholars of the reports about the prophets said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent two envoys from among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) to Antioch (Anṭākiya). When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending a few sheep, and he was Ḥabīb, the companion of Yā-Sīn. They greeted him, and the old man said: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus, calling you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes, we heal the sick and we cure the blind from birth and the leper, by God's permission." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill and bedridden for years." They said: "Then take us to your house, so we may see his condition."

He brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and at that moment he stood up healthy by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God healed many of the sick through their hands. The people had a king called Sallāḥīn.

He said: His name was Abṭayḥīs, one of the kings of the Romans, who worshipped idols. They said: The news reached him and he summoned them. He said to them: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "We cure the blind from birth and the leper, and we heal the sick, by God's permission." He said: "And for what did you come?" They said: "We came to call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees." The king said: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "Wait until I consider your matter." So the people followed them, seized them, and beat them in the marketplace.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent these two envoys to Antioch. They arrived there but did not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they glorified God and remembered Him. The king became angry, ordered them seized and imprisoned, and each of them was given one hundred lashes. They said: When the two envoys were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the head of the disciples, Shim'ūn al-Ṣafā (Simon Peter), after them to support them.

Shim'ūn entered the city disguised and began to associate with the king's retinue until they grew fond of him. His news was raised to the king, who summoned him, was pleased with his company, grew fond of him, and honored him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to other than your religion. Did you speak with them and hear their words?"

The king said: "Anger prevented me from that." He said: "Then, if the king sees fit, let him summon them so we may find out what they have."

The king summoned them, and Shim'ūn said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'ūn said: "Then describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and judges what He desires." Shim'ūn said: "And what is your sign?" They said to him: "Ask whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes were effaced, the place of his eyes like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight was split open. Then they took two balls of clay and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs, and he saw with them. The king marveled, and Shim'ūn said to the king: "Have you seen? If you asked your god to do the like of this, there would be honor for you and for your god."

The king said to him: "There is no secret with me. Our god that we worship neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Whenever the king entered the idol's place, Shim'ūn would enter with him, pray much, and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed.

The king said to the two envoys: "If your god whom you worship has power to revive the dead, we will believe in Him and in you." They said: "Our God is powerful over everything." The king said: "Here there is a dead man, the son of a landowner (dihqān), who died seven days ago. I have delayed burying him until his father returns, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, who had changed and begun to smell. They called upon their Lord openly, and Shim'ūn called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I died seven days ago, and I found a polytheist, so I was put into nine valleys of Fire. I warn you of what you are in; so believe in God."

Then he said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I looked and saw a youth of fair face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'ūn and these two," and he pointed to his two companions. The king marveled. When Shim'ūn knew that his word had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and invited him, and a group believed, and the king was among those who believed, while others disbelieved.

Ibn Isḥāq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people agreed to kill the envoys. This reached Ḥabīb, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the envoys. This is His saying, glorified is He: "When We sent to them two." 

They differed about their names. Ibn 'Abbās said: Tārūṣ and Mārūṣ. Wahb said: Yaḥyā and Yūnus. Muqātil said: Tūmān and Mānūṣ.

"But they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third." That is, We strengthened them with a third envoy. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and 'Āṣim, according to Ḥafṣ, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light pronunciation (fa-ʿazaznā, i.e., "so We overpowered"), from ʿazīz (mighty), meaning: "so We overpowered them," with a third envoy, who was Shim'ūn.

Muqātil said: Shim'ān. Ka'b said: The two envoys were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq, and the third was Shalūm. He attributed the sending to Himself because Jesus (peace be upon him) sent them only by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, and they were among the envoys. They all said to the people of Antioch: "Indeed, we are sent to you." They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying." That is, you are only liars. They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you. And our duty is only the clear conveyance." They said: "Indeed, we consider you an omen."

"[Your] omen is with you." Muqātil said: rain was withheld from them, and they said: "This is because of your ill omen." "If you do not desist, we will surely stone you." Qatādah said: with stones. Others said: we will kill you. "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us." They said: "Your omen is with you": your ill omen is with you because of your disbelief. Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: your share of good and evil.

Qatādah said: your deeds. And al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj recited "ṭayrukum" (your bird).

"Even if you are reminded?" That is, admonished. Abū Ja'far recited it with light pronunciation, meaning: because you were reminded. Its answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "Even if you are reminded, you say this?" "Rather, you are a people who are transgressing": polytheists exceeding the limit.

His saying: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city." He was Ḥabīb ibn Maryam. Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil said: Ḥabīb ibn Isrā'īl the carpenter (al-Najjār). Wahb said: He was a sickly man whose leprosy had spread, and his house was at the farthest gate of the city. He was a believer and charitable; he gathered his earnings in the evening and divided them into two halves: he fed his family one half and gave the other half in charity. When it reached him that his people intended to kill the envoys, he came to them and said:

"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both. "And what their hands made": the majority recited it with a hā'; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa recited "ʿamilat" without the hā'. "Mā" may be read in three ways:

The first: negation, meaning "and their hands did not make it"; that is, they found it made, and they had no hand in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil.

The second: the masdar sense, meaning "and from the work of their hands."

The third: the sense of "that which" (alladhī), [meaning "and that which their hands made"] of the tilling, planting, and grafting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. "Will they not give thanks" for His blessings?

"Glory be to Him who created the pairs" — the kinds and types — "all of them, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know. And a sign for them is the night: We strip off (naslakh) from it the day," that is, We remove and extract the day from it. Al-Kalbī said: "We take it away," "and behold, they are in darkness," that is, entering into the dark.

"And the sun runs on to a resting place for it," meaning toward its stationary point. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It does not reach its resting place until it returns to its stations. Qatādah said: until a fixed time for it that it does not exceed. It was said: until the end of its affair at the ending of the world. It was said: to its furthest setting-point.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Ibrāhīm ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bakkār al-ʿĪsī narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, saying: Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne." [75] [[Musnad Aḥmad: 5/158.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

And strike for them a parable: the people of the town, when the messengers came to it. The messengers here are the envoys of Jesus. The scholars of the reports about the prophets said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent two envoys from among the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) to Antioch (Anṭākiya). When they drew near the city, they saw an old man tending a few sheep, and he was Ḥabīb, the companion of Yā-Sīn. They greeted him, and the old man said: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus, calling you from the worship of idols to the worship of the Most Merciful." He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "Yes, we heal the sick and we cure the blind from birth and the leper, by God's permission." The old man said: "I have a son who has been ill and bedridden for years." They said: "Then take us to your house, so we may see his condition."

He brought them to his house, and they wiped over his son, and at that moment he stood up healthy by God's permission. The news spread through the city, and God healed many of the sick through their hands. The people had a king called Sallāḥīn.

He said: His name was Abṭayḥīs, one of the kings of the Romans, who worshipped idols. They said: The news reached him and he summoned them. He said to them: "Who are you two?" They said: "We are the envoys of Jesus." He said: "And what is your sign?" They said: "We cure the blind from birth and the leper, and we heal the sick, by God's permission." He said: "And for what did you come?" They said: "We came to call you from worshipping what neither hears nor sees to worshipping Him who hears and sees." The king said: "Do we have a god other than our gods?" They said: "Yes, the One who created you and your gods." He said: "Wait until I consider your matter." So the people followed them, seized them, and beat them in the marketplace.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Jesus (peace be upon him) sent these two envoys to Antioch. They arrived there but did not reach its king, and their stay was prolonged. One day the king went out, and they glorified God and remembered Him. The king became angry, ordered them seized and imprisoned, and each of them was given one hundred lashes. They said: When the two envoys were denied and beaten, Jesus sent the head of the disciples, Shim'ūn al-Ṣafā (Simon Peter), after them to support them.

Shim'ūn entered the city disguised and began to associate with the king's retinue until they grew fond of him. His news was raised to the king, who summoned him, was pleased with his company, grew fond of him, and honored him. Then one day he said to him: "O King, it has reached me that you imprisoned two men and beat them when they called you to other than your religion. Did you speak with them and hear their words?"

The king said: "Anger prevented me from that." He said: "Then, if the king sees fit, let him summon them so we may find out what they have."

The king summoned them, and Shim'ūn said to them: "Who sent you here?" They said: "God, who created everything, and has no partner." Shim'ūn said: "Then describe Him, and be brief." They said: "He does what He wills and judges what He desires." Shim'ūn said: "And what is your sign?" They said to him: "Ask whatever you wish." So the king ordered that they bring a boy whose eyes were effaced, the place of his eyes like a forehead. They kept calling upon their Lord until the place of sight was split open. Then they took two balls of clay and placed them in his eye sockets, and they became two eyeballs, and he saw with them. The king marveled, and Shim'ūn said to the king: "Have you seen? If you asked your god to do the like of this, there would be honor for you and for your god."

The king said to him: "There is no secret with me. Our god that we worship neither sees, nor hears, nor harms, nor benefits." Whenever the king entered the idol's place, Shim'ūn would enter with him, pray much, and humble himself, until they thought he was of their creed.

The king said to the two envoys: "If your god whom you worship has power to revive the dead, we will believe in Him and in you." They said: "Our God is powerful over everything." The king said: "Here there is a dead man, the son of a landowner (dihqān), who died seven days ago. I have delayed burying him until his father returns, for he was absent." They brought the dead man, who had changed and begun to smell. They called upon their Lord openly, and Shim'ūn called upon his Lord in secret. The dead man stood up and said: "I died seven days ago, and I found a polytheist, so I was put into nine valleys of Fire. I warn you of what you are in; so believe in God."

Then he said: "The gates of heaven were opened, and I looked and saw a youth of fair face interceding for these three." The king said: "And who are the three?" He said: "Shim'ūn and these two," and he pointed to his two companions. The king marveled. When Shim'ūn knew that his word had affected the king, he informed him of the situation and invited him, and a group believed, and the king was among those who believed, while others disbelieved.

Ibn Isḥāq said, on the authority of Ka'b and Wahb: Rather, the king disbelieved, and he and his people agreed to kill the envoys. This reached Ḥabīb, who was at the farthest gate of the city. He came running to them, reminding them and calling them to obey the envoys. This is His saying, glorified is He: "When We sent to them two." 

They differed about their names. Ibn 'Abbās said: Tārūṣ and Mārūṣ. Wahb said: Yaḥyā and Yūnus. Muqātil said: Tūmān and Mānūṣ.

"But they denied them, so We strengthened [them] with a third." That is, We strengthened them with a third envoy. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and 'Āṣim, according to Ḥafṣ, recited "fa-'azzaznā" with a light pronunciation (fa-ʿazaznā, i.e., "so We overpowered"), from ʿazīz (mighty), meaning: "so We overpowered them," with a third envoy, who was Shim'ūn.

Muqātil said: Shim'ān. Ka'b said: The two envoys were Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq, and the third was Shalūm. He attributed the sending to Himself because Jesus (peace be upon him) sent them only by the command of the Mighty and Majestic, and they were among the envoys. They all said to the people of Antioch: "Indeed, we are sent to you." They said: "You are only human beings like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying." That is, you are only liars. They said: "Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you. And our duty is only the clear conveyance." They said: "Indeed, we consider you an omen."

"[Your] omen is with you." Muqātil said: rain was withheld from them, and they said: "This is because of your ill omen." "If you do not desist, we will surely stone you." Qatādah said: with stones. Others said: we will kill you. "And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us." They said: "Your omen is with you": your ill omen is with you because of your disbelief. Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: your share of good and evil.

Qatādah said: your deeds. And al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj recited "ṭayrukum" (your bird).

"Even if you are reminded?" That is, admonished. Abū Ja'far recited it with light pronunciation, meaning: because you were reminded. Its answer is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "Even if you are reminded, you say this?" "Rather, you are a people who are transgressing": polytheists exceeding the limit.

His saying: "A man came running from the farthest part of the city." He was Ḥabīb ibn Maryam. Ibn 'Abbās and Muqātil said: Ḥabīb ibn Isrā'īl the carpenter (al-Najjār). Wahb said: He was a sickly man whose leprosy had spread, and his house was at the farthest gate of the city. He was a believer and charitable; he gathered his earnings in the evening and divided them into two halves: he fed his family one half and gave the other half in charity. When it reached him that his people intended to kill the envoys, he came to them and said:

"O my people, follow the envoys. Follow those who do not ask you for any wage, and they are guided." Qatādah said: When Ḥabīb reached the envoys, he said to them: "Do you ask any wage for this?" They said: "No." So he said that. He said: Ḥabīb had been in a cave worshipping his Lord. When the news of the envoys reached him, he came to them and manifested his religion and what he was upon of monotheism and the worship of God. It was said to him: "You oppose our religion and follow the religion of these envoys and believe in their god?" He said: "And why should I not worship Him who created me, and to Him you will be returned? Shall I take gods besides Him, if the Most Merciful wills harm for me, their intercession will not avail me at all, nor can they rescue me? Indeed, if I did that, I would be in clear error. Indeed, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me."

When he said that to them, they rushed at him in one single rush and killed him, and no one defended him. 

'Abd Allāh ibn Mas'ūd said: They trampled him with their feet until his intestine came out from his anus. Al-Suddī said: They threw stones at him while he said: "O God, guide my people," until they cut him up and killed him. Al-Ḥasan said: They made holes in a rope-ring, hung him from the market of the city, and his grave is in the wall of Antioch. God made Paradise obligatory for him, and that is His saying: "It was said: Enter Paradise."

When he reached the Garden of God and His honor, he said: "Would that my people knew, by what my Lord has forgiven me and made me among the honored."

Abū Bakr 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Alī ibn Ḥamshād al-Muzakkī informed us, by my reading to him in Sha'bān of the year four hundred, and he affirmed it, saying: Abū Ẓahīr 'Abd Allāh ibn Fāris ibn Muḥammad ibn 'Alī ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb informed us in Rabī' al-Awwal of the year three hundred and six and four, saying: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl ibn Mālik narrated to us from his brother ʿĪsā, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The foremost of the nations are three, who did not disbelieve in God for the blink of an eye: 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the companion of the family of Yā-Sīn, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh. They are the truthful ones (ṣiddīqūn), and 'Alī is the best of them." [74] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmāl: 11/601, no. 32898; Tafsīr Majmaʿ al-Bayān: 8/269; Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī: 15/20, where it reads: "The truthful ones are three: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, the believer of the family of Yā-Sīn; Ḥizqīl, the believer of the family of Pharaoh; and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who is the best of them."]].

They said: When Ḥabīb was killed, God became angry on his behalf and hastened retribution against them. He commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him), who cried out at them with one cry, and they all died to the last of them. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "And We did not send down upon his people after him any host from heaven, nor were We ever going to send [one]. It was but one cry (ṣayḥa)." In the codex of 'Abd Allāh: "It was but one zaqiyya," which is also a cry, and its root is from zaqā (to cry out). Abū Ja'far recited "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative ending, making the verb kāna mean "happened." "Then they were extinguished," meaning dead.

"Oh, the anguish upon the servants!" 'Ikrima said: That is, upon themselves. There are two views on this:

The first: God says: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," and a sorrow upon them when they did not believe.

The second: It is the speech of those who perished. Abū al-ʿĀliya said: When they witnessed the punishment, they said: "Oh, the anguish upon the servants," meaning the three envoys, because they had not believed in them, so they wished for faith when it no longer benefited them. ʿIkrima recited "yā ḥasrah" with the hā' pronounced as a pause (ḥasrah → ḥasrah). "No messenger comes to them but that they used to mock him."

The account of the three envoys was in the days of the petty kings (mulūk al-ṭawāʾif).

"Have they not seen": that is, the people of Mecca, "how many generations We destroyed before them?" The qarn (generation) is the people of each era, and they were so called because of their closeness in existence. "That they will not return to them." 

"And all of them, when": with the doubled mīm (lammā), recited by Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Ḥamza. The rest recited it with a single mīm. Whoever doubled it made "in" (in) mean negation, and "lammā" mean "only," the sense being: "And every one is only all gathered together," like their saying: "I asked you why you did it," meaning: only did you do it. Whoever lightened it made "in" for emphasis, and "mā" is extra, the sense being: "And all of them are indeed brought before Us."

"And a sign for them is the dead earth, which We have revived with rain, and We have brought forth from it grain, of which they eat. And We have made in it gardens (jannāt)": gardens of palm trees and grapes, "and We have caused springs to gush forth in it, so that they may eat of its fruit." Al-Aʿmash recited "thumrihi" with a ḍamma on the thā' and a sukūn on the mīm (thumrihi). Khalaf, Yaḥyā, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī recited it with a ḍamma on both the thā' and the mīm, and the others recited it with a fatḥa on both. "And what their hands made": the majority recited it with a hā'; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and the people of Kufa recited "ʿamilat" without the hā'. "Mā" may be read in three ways:

The first: negation, meaning "and their hands did not make it"; that is, they found it made, and they had no hand in it. This is the view of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil.

The second: the masdar sense, meaning "and from the work of their hands."

The third: the sense of "that which" (alladhī), [meaning "and that which their hands made"] of the tilling, planting, and grafting. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās. "Will they not give thanks" for His blessings?

"Glory be to Him who created the pairs" — the kinds and types — "all of them, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know. And a sign for them is the night: We strip off (naslakh) from it the day," that is, We remove and extract the day from it. Al-Kalbī said: "We take it away," "and behold, they are in darkness," that is, entering into the dark.

"And the sun runs on to a resting place for it," meaning toward its stationary point. Ibn ʿAbbās said: It does not reach its resting place until it returns to its stations. Qatādah said: until a fixed time for it that it does not exceed. It was said: until the end of its affair at the ending of the world. It was said: to its furthest setting-point.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Aḥmad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, both saying: Ibrāhīm ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bakkār al-ʿĪsī narrated to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, saying: Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, from his father, from Abū Dharr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning His saying: "And the sun runs on to a resting place for it." He said: "Its resting place is beneath the Throne." [75] [[Musnad Aḥmad: 5/158.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Ḥabīsh narrated to us, saying: Abū al-Ṭayyib Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yaḥyā al-Dārimī narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿAbd Allāh Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Samarqandī narrated to us in Damietta, saying: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām narrated to us, saying: Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Ḥassān, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he recited: "And the sun runs, there is no resting place for it" (wa-l-shamsu tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā). This is also the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, meaning: it has no rest; so it is always running.

"That is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing." "And the moon": with a nominative ending (wa-l-qamaru), recited by Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ayyūb, and Yaʿqūb, except Warsh (Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Maqrī al-Warshī al-Maghribī al-Andalusī). Abū Ḥātim preferred this, saying: "Because you have diverted the verb from it, so you have raised it as the subject (mubtada')." The rest recited it with a fatḥa, and Abū ʿUbayd preferred this, saying: "Because of the verb preceding it and following it. As for the preceding one, it is His saying: 'We strip from it the day.' As for the following one, it is His saying: 'We have determined it'" (qaddarnāhu), meaning: We determined for it the stations.

"Stations": that is, We determined for it the stations, which are twenty-eight stations, in each of which the moon descends one night. Their names are: al-Sharṭān, al-Biṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-ʿAwwā, al-Simāk, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Baldah, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Farāgh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and Baṭn al-Ḥūt.

"Until he returns like the old date-stalk (ʿurjūn)": it is the palm-branch on which the clusters are; when it becomes old and dries, it bends and turns yellow. The moon is likened to it in its thinness and yellowness. It is also called al-Ahān.

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon," but rather both travel ceaselessly, and each has a limit it does not exceed or fall short of. When the authority of this one comes, that one goes, and when the authority of that one comes, this one goes. That is His saying: "Nor does the night outstrip the day." When both meet and each one overtakes the other, the Resurrection will occur, and that is His saying, glorified is He: "And the sun and moon are joined together."

"And each in an orbit is swimming": they are moving.

"And a sign for them: that We carried their offspring in the laden ship" — the loaded, full ship. It is the ship of Noah: the forefathers in the ship, and the descendants in the loins. Ḥaml (carrying) means preventing a thing from going downward.

"And We created for them of its like what they ride": that is, of the like of Noah's ship, the boats, all of them.

Ubayd ibn Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Mahdī informed us, saying: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Mūsā narrated to us, from Sufyān, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik, concerning His saying: "And We created for them of its like what they ride." He said: "Small boats." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Camels are the ships of the land."

"And if We will, We drown them, and there is no shout for them, nor are they rescued," that is, they are saved from drowning. "Except as a mercy from Us and an enjoyment for a time," meaning until the completion of their terms.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah Ya-Sin (36), verses 45–59**

﴿And when it is said to them, "Beware of what is before you and what is behind you, so that you may be shown mercy"...﴾ That is, "what is before you" means the Hereafter: act for it. "And what is behind you" means the affairs of this world: be wary of them and do not be deceived by them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: "What is before you" is the sins that will come, and "what is behind you" is the sins that have passed.

al-Hasan said: "What is before you" means the events of God concerning those who came before you from the nations, and "what is behind you" means the matter of the Hour.

Muqatil said: "What is before you" is the punishment of the past nations, and "what is behind you" is the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿...so that you may be shown mercy.﴾ The response is omitted, and its estimate is: when this is said to them, they turn away. Its evidence is what follows: ﴿Not a sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾

﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom God would have fed if He had willed?"﴾ They imagine that since God is able to feed him and does not will to feed him, we have a better claim to that. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah when the poor companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them, "Give us some of what you claim from your wealth is for God." That is His saying: ﴿And they assign to God a portion of what He has produced of crops and livestock﴾ [al-An'am 6:136]. They denied them, and said, "If God willed, He would have fed you, so we will not give you anything until you return to our religion."

﴿You are only in clear error,﴾ in following Muhammad and opposing our religion. This is related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and others said it is the words of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to them.

﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ That is, "When will we be resurrected?" God the Exalted said: ﴿They await only a single blast, which will seize them while they are disputing﴾, and it is the blast of Israfil. The phrase "while they are disputing" means they argue, and some of them contend with others.

The readers differed concerning it. Ibn Kathir, Warsh, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim read it with a fatha on the *kha'* and a shadda on the *sad* (Arabic: *yakhessimun* as *yakhassamun*), and Hisham related the same from the people of Syria. When they assimilated the letters, they transferred the vowel of the *ta'* to the *kha'*.

Abu Ja'far, Ayyub and Nafi' (other than Warsh) read it with a sukun on the *kha'* and a light *sad*. Abu 'Amr read it with *ikhfa'* (concealment). Hamza read it with a sukun on the *kha'* and a light *sad*, meaning that some of them overcome others in disputing. This is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. The rest read it with a kasra on the *kha'* and a shadda on the *sad*.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their families.﴾ That is, they will not be able to direct one another in a will, nor to return to their families.

﴿And the Horn will be blown,﴾ and this is the final blast, the blast of resurrection. Between the two blasts is forty years. ﴿Then they will emerge from the graves (al-ajdath) to their Lord, hastening,﴾ that is, they will come out. al-Ajdath means the graves, and its singular is *jadath*. Their saying "naslan" to a child derives from this, because it comes out from its mother's womb. *Al-nasalan* and *al-'aslan* mean hastening in walking.

﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?"﴾ That is, from our sleep. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: They say this only because God lifted the punishment from them between the two blasts, so they sleep. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: when the disbelievers see Hell and its various torments, what they were punished with in the graves becomes like sleep beside it, so they say, "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" Then He says: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth.﴾ They acknowledge it when acknowledgment no longer benefits them.

Mujahid said: The disbelievers say, "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" and the believers say, "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."

﴿It will be only a single blast, and then they will all be brought before Us.﴾ ﴿So today no soul will be wronged in the least, and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do.﴾ The place of *ma* (what) is in the accusative for two reasons:
One: it is the object of a passive verb whose subject is unnamed (*ma lam yusamma fa'iluh*).
The second: it is by removal of a preposition (*harf al-khafd*) [in the original: "the attribute"], meaning *bi-ma* (with what).

﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joyful occupation.﴾ Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Shaybah read the *ghayn* with a sukun, which Abu Hatim preferred. The others read it with a damma, which Abu 'Ubayd preferred. Both are dialects, like *as-suht* and *as-suht* and similar words.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of "shughl" (occupation). Muhammad ibn Hamdun informed us: Makki ibn 'Abdan informed us: Abu al-Azhar told us: Asbat ibn Muhammad told us, from his father, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joyful occupation﴾ that he said: "the deflowering of virgins."

Fanjawayh informed me: 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf told us: Ahmad ibn al-Walid al-Shatawi told us: Muhammad ibn Musa told us: Mu'alla ibn 'Abd al-Rahman told us: Shurayk told us, from 'Asim al-Ahwal, from Abu al-Mutawakkil al-Naji, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the people of the Garden have intercourse with their wives, they return to being virgins."

al-Kalbi, al-Thumali and al-Musayyib said: it means they are occupied, away from the people of the Fire and from what they are in; their concerns do not trouble them and they do not remember them. Waki' ibn al-Jarrah said: it means in listening (*al-sama'*). Yahya ibn Mu'adh was asked: "Which voices are the most beautiful?" He said: "The flutes of intimacy in the chambers of holiness, with melodies of adornment in the gardens of glorification, ﴿in a seat of truth, near a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾" [al-Qamar 54:55].

Ibn Kaysan said: it means in visiting one another. It was said: in the hospitality of God. It was also said: their occupation is with ten things: a kingship with no deposition, a youth with no old age, a health with no sickness, a might with no humiliation, a rest with no hardship, a blessing with no affliction, a survival with no death, a life with no dying, a contentment with no anger, and an intimacy with no loneliness.

It was said: their occupation in the Garden is with seven kinds of reward for seven limbs. As for the reward of the foot, it is His saying: ﴿Enter it in peace, secure﴾ [al-Hijr 15:46]. The reward of the hand is His saying: ﴿They will pass around a cup﴾ [al-Tur 52:23]. The reward of the private part is His saying: ﴿And wide-eyed maidens﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:22]. The reward of the belly is His saying: ﴿Eat and drink with satisfaction﴾ [al-Tur 52:19], etc. The reward of the tongue is His saying: ﴿And the last of their call is, "Praise to God, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus 10:10]. The reward of the ear is His saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech or sin, only the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:25–26]. The reward of the eye is His saying: ﴿and the eyes will be delighted﴾.

Tawus said: If the people of the Garden knew what they were preoccupied from, what they are occupied with would not delight them.

A wise man was asked about the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Most of the people of the Garden are the simple (al-bulh)." He said: "Because they are occupied with the bliss from the Bestower of bliss." Then he said: "Whoever is content with the Garden in place of God is simple (ableh)."

﴿Fakihun﴾: the common readers recite it with an *alif*. Abu Ja'far read *fakihun* and *fakihin* without an *alif* wherever they occur. Both are dialects, like *al-hadhir* and *al-hadhr*, and *al-farih* and *al-fareh*. al-Kisa'i said: *al-fakih* and *al-fakiha* are like *shahim* and *lahim*, and *laban* and *tamir*. The scholars differed concerning their meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said: joyful (*farihun*). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: admiring/pleased (*mu'jabun*). al-Suddi said: at ease (*na'imun*).

﴿They and their spouses,﴾ that is, their wives, ﴿in shade,﴾ the common readers recite *zilal* with an *alif* and a kasra on the *zay* [*zilal*], as the plural of *zill* (shade). Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *zulal* as the plural of *zullah*.

﴿Reclining on couches,﴾ that is, beds within canopies. Its singular is *arikah*, like *safinah* and *safin* and *safa'in*. It was said: they are cushions. ﴿They will have therein fruit, and they will have whatever they call for.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: they ask for. Muqatil said: they wish for and desire. It was said: its meaning is that whoever claims anything of them, it is theirs by the judgment of God the Mighty and Majestic, because they claim only what is good.

﴿Peace (salam)﴾: the common readers recite it in the nominative, meaning "for them is peace." al-Nakha'i read it in the accusative, as an absolute/adverbial construction (*al-qat' wa al-masdar*).

al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hafiz informed me: Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan told us: Ahmad ibn al-Faraj al-Muqri' told us: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Malik Abu al-Shawarib told us: Abu 'Asim 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Abbadani told us: al-Fadl ibn 'Isa al-Raqqashi told us. And 'Abd al-Khaliq ibn 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Khaliq al-Mu'adhdhin informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Musa al-Mulhimi al-Isfahani told me: al-Hasan ibn Abi 'Ali al-Za'farani told us: Ibn Abi al-Shawarib told us: Abu 'Asim told us: al-Fadl al-Raqqashi told us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"While the people of the Garden are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, and they raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has looked down upon them from above, and said: 'Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden.' That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿A word from a Lord, Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:58]. So He looks at them and they look at Him, and they do not turn to anything of the bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and blessing remain upon them in their abodes."

Mujahid said: "What is before you" is the sins that will come, and "what is behind you" is the sins that have passed.

al-Hasan said: "What is before you" means the events of God concerning those who came before you from the nations, and "what is behind you" means the matter of the Hour.

Muqatil said: "What is before you" is the punishment of the past nations, and "what is behind you" is the punishment of the Hereafter.

﴿...so that you may be shown mercy.﴾ The response is omitted, and its estimate is: when this is said to them, they turn away. Its evidence is what follows: ﴿Not a sign comes to them from the signs of their Lord except that they turn away from it.﴾

﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend from what God has provided you," those who disbelieve say to those who believe, "Shall we feed one whom God would have fed if He had willed?"﴾ They imagine that since God is able to feed him and does not will to feed him, we have a better claim to that. It was revealed concerning the polytheists of Makkah when the poor companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them, "Give us some of what you claim from your wealth is for God." That is His saying: ﴿And they assign to God a portion of what He has produced of crops and livestock﴾ [al-An'am 6:136]. They denied them, and said, "If God willed, He would have fed you, so we will not give you anything until you return to our religion."

﴿You are only in clear error,﴾ in following Muhammad and opposing our religion. This is related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and others said it is the words of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to them.

The readers differed concerning it. When they assimilated the letters, they transferred the vowel of the *ta'* to the *kha'*.

Hamza read it with a sukun on the *kha'* and a light *sad*, meaning that some of them overcome others in disputing. This is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. The rest read it with a kasra on the *kha'* and a shadda on the *sad*.

﴿So they will not be able to make a bequest, nor will they return to their families.﴾ That is, they will not be able to direct one another in a will, nor to return to their families.

﴿And the Horn will be blown,﴾ and this is the final blast, the blast of resurrection. Between the two blasts is forty years. ﴿Then they will emerge from the graves (al-ajdath) to their Lord, hastening,﴾ that is, they will come out. al-Ajdath means the graves, and its singular is *jadath*. Their saying "naslan" to a child derives from this, because it comes out from its mother's womb. *Al-nasalan* and *al-'aslan* mean hastening in walking.

﴿They will say, "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?"﴾ That is, from our sleep. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: They say this only because God lifted the punishment from them between the two blasts, so they sleep. The reward of the belly is His saying: ﴿Eat and drink with satisfaction﴾ [al-Tur 52:19], etc. The reward of the tongue is His saying: ﴿And the last of their call is, "Praise to God, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus 10:10]. The reward of the ear is His saying: ﴿They will not hear therein any ill speech or sin, only the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:25–26]. The reward of the eye is His saying: ﴿and the eyes will be delighted﴾.

Tawus said: If the people of the Garden knew what they were preoccupied from, what they are occupied with would not delight them.

A wise man was asked about the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Most of the people of the Garden are the simple (al-bulh)." He said: "Because they are occupied with the bliss from the Bestower of bliss." Then he said: "Whoever is content with the Garden in place of God is simple (ableh)."

﴿Fakihun﴾: the common readers recite it with an *alif*. Abu Ja'far read *fakihun* and *fakihin* without an *alif* wherever they occur. Both are dialects, like *al-hadhir* and *al-hadhr*, and *al-farih* and *al-fareh*. al-Kisa'i said: *al-fakih* and *al-fakiha* are like *shahim* and *lahim*, and *laban* and *tamir*. The scholars differed concerning their meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said: joyful (*farihun*). Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: admiring/pleased (*mu'jabun*). al-Suddi said: at ease (*na'imun*).

﴿They and their spouses,﴾ that is, their wives, ﴿in shade,﴾ the common readers recite *zilal* with an *alif* and a kasra on the *zay* [*zilal*], as the plural of *zill* (shade). Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *zulal* as the plural of *zullah*.

﴿Reclining on couches,﴾ that is, beds within canopies. Its singular is *arikah*, like *safinah* and *safin* and *safa'in*. It was said: they are cushions. ﴿They will have therein fruit, and they will have whatever they call for.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: they ask for. Muqatil said: they wish for and desire. It was said: its meaning is that whoever claims anything of them, it is theirs by the judgment of God the Mighty and Majestic, because they claim only what is good.

﴿Peace (salam)﴾: the common readers recite it in the nominative, meaning "for them is peace." al-Nakha'i read it in the accusative, as an absolute/adverbial construction (*al-qat' wa al-masdar*).

al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hafiz informed me: Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan told us: Ahmad ibn al-Faraj al-Muqri' told us: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Malik Abu al-Shawarib told us: Abu 'Asim 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Abbadani told us: al-Fadl ibn 'Isa al-Raqqashi told us. And 'Abd al-Khaliq ibn 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Khaliq al-Mu'adhdhin informed us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Musa al-Mulhimi al-Isfahani told me: al-Hasan ibn Abi 'Ali al-Za'farani told us: Ibn Abi al-Shawarib told us: Abu 'Asim told us: al-Fadl al-Raqqashi told us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"While the people of the Garden are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, and they raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, has looked down upon them from above, and said: 'Peace be upon you, O people of the Garden.' That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿A word from a Lord, Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:58]. So He looks at them and they look at Him, and they do not turn to anything of the bliss as long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and blessing remain upon them in their abodes."

﴿And, "Stand apart today, O criminals!"﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Separate yourselves." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "Be distinguished." al-Suddi said: "Be on your own." Qatadah said: "Turn away from every good." al-Dahhak said: For every disbeliever in the Fire there is a house; he enters that house, and it is sealed over him with fire, so he remains in it forever and is neither seen nor sees.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 36, verses 60–83:

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan? Indeed, he is a clear enemy to you. And that you should worship Me; this is a straight path.﴾ "Not worship Satan" means: do not obey him in disobedience to God. ﴿And he had already misled a great multitude from among you.﴾ That is, he led them astray by calling them to disobedience.

Ali (may God be pleased with him) read ﴿jibillan﴾ with a ba' and light (mukhaffaf) pronunciation. The people of Madina, ʿAsim, Ayyub, Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim read it with kasra on the jim and the ba', and with shadda on the lam. Yaʿqub read it with damma on the jim and the ba', and with shadda on the lam; this is also how al-Hasan, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and al-Ashhab read it. Ibn ʿAmir and Abu ʿAmr read it with damma on the jim, sukun on the ba', and light pronunciation of the lam. The rest read it with damma on the jim and the ba', and light pronunciation of the lam. All of these are dialectal variants (lughat).

Its meaning is: creation and community (umma). Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose damma on the jim and the ba' with shadda on the lam, because of God's saying: ﴿and the earlier generations﴾ [[Surat al-Shu'ara': 184.]].

﴿Did you not then use your reason?﴾ ﴿This is Hell, which you were promised.﴾ ﴿Burn therein﴾: enter it. ﴿today, for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ ﴿Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾ Qatada said: disputes and speech took place among them, and this was the last of it.

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn al-Husayn informed me, saying: Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan related to us, saying: Abu ʿAmir Hamid ibn Sa'dan related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Salih related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Wahb related to us, saying:

ʿAmr ibn al-Harith related to me, from Darraj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, the disbeliever will be made to recognize his deeds, and he will deny and dispute. It will be said to him: 'These are your neighbours, bearing witness.' He will say: 'They lie.' It will be said: 'Your family and your kinsfolk.' He will say: 'They lie.' It will be said: 'Swear.' And they will swear.

Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, will silence them, and their tongues will bear witness against them, and then He will send them into the Fire." [79] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 10/351.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Shanba related to us, saying: al-Firyabi related to us, saying: Hisham ibn ʿAmmar related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn ʿAyyash related to us, saying: Damdam ibn Zur'a related to me, from Shurayh ibn ʿUbayd, from ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "The first part of a person to speak on the day the mouths are sealed is his thigh, from the left leg." [80] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/151.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: al-Qati'i related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal related to us, saying: my father related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: al-Hariri Abu Mas'ud informed us, from Hakim ibn Mu'awiya ibn Haydah, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "They will come on the Day of Resurrection with fadam (seals) upon their mouths, and the first of the sons of Adam to speak will be his thigh and his palm." [81] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/3, with variation.]]

﴿And their hands will speak to Us and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes, so they would race toward the path; but how could they see?﴾ "Fastabaqu al-sirat": they would hasten to the road. ﴿How then could they see?﴾ since We had obliterated their eyes. Ibn ʿAbbas, Muqatil, ʿAta' and Qatada said: this means that if We willed, We would have left them blind, wandering about, so how could they see the path at that time?

﴿And if We willed, We would have transformed them where they stood﴾: that is, We would have made them sit in their dwellings as apes and swine. Maskh is the changing of a form. ﴿So they would not be able to proceed, nor return﴾ to what they were before. It was also said: they would be unable to go forward or to return.

﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation.﴾ Al-A'mash, ʿAsim and Hamza read it with shadda; others read it with fatha on the nun and damma on the kaf, light pronunciation. That is, He returns him ﴿to the most abject age﴾, likening his state to that of a child, who is the beginning of creation. It was also said: He turns him, after strength, to weakness, and after growth to decline, and after vigour and freshness to decay and frailty, so it is as if his state were reversed.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Habish the reciter related to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Mihran ibn Abi ʿUmar related to us, from Sufyan: ﴿And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾, he said: when he reaches eighty years, his body changes. ﴿Will they not then use their reason?﴾

﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him﴾, because it would give rise to doubt.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Hamid ibn Shu'ayb related to us, from Shurayh ibn Yunus, saying: Yahya ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abi ʿUyayna related to us, from his father, from al-Hakam, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to quote the verse of al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas:

"Will you make my plunder and the plunder of the slaves equal to al-Aqra' and ʿUyayna?"

They said: "O Messenger of God, he only said: '... between ʿUyayna and al-Aqra'.'" He repeated it and said: "between al-Aqra' and ʿUyayna." Then Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with him) stood up, kissed his head, and said: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him﴾ [82] [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/268, with variation.]]

Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Hadithi informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Hamdan related to us, saying: Yusuf ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Hamman related to us, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama related to us, from ʿAli ibn Zayd, from al-Hasan, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to quote this line:

"Islam and grey hair are sufficient as a restraint for a man."

Abu Bakr said: "O Prophet of God, the poet only said:

'Grey hair and Islam are sufficient as a restraint for a man.'"

Then Abu Bakr or ʿUmar said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God; God the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him﴾." [[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/585.]]

Al-Husayn informed me, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Musayyabi related to us, saying: Hamid ibn Shu'ayb related to us, saying: Shurayh ibn Yunus related to us, saying: Abu Sufyan related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And We did not teach him poetry﴾: it has reached me that ʿAʾisha was asked whether the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to quote anything of poetry. She said:

"Poetry was the most hateful speech to him." She said: "He quoted nothing of poetry except the verse of the brother of the tribe of Bani Qays, Tarafa:

'The days will reveal to you what you did not know, and there will come to you news from one who did not provide you'" [[Lisan al-ʿArab: 13/259.]]

He began to say: "from one who did not provide you (lam tuzawwid) with news." Abu Bakr said: "It is not like this, O Messenger of God." He (ﷺ) said: "I am not a poet, nor is it fitting for me." [83] [[Kashf al-Khafa': 1/448.]]

﴿It is only a reminder and a clear Qur'an﴾, ﴿that it may warn﴾ — with the ta' (tunedhira), which is the reading of the people of Madina, Syria and Basra except Abu ʿAmr; the rest read it with the ya' (yunedhira). He said: the ta' refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the ya' refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Whoever is alive﴾: that is, sensible and a believer in God's knowledge, since the disbeliever and the ignorant are dead of heart, ﴿and the word will be fulfilled against the disbelievers.﴾

﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our hands have made, cattle, and they are masters over them?﴾ That is: We made them without intermediary, agent, or partner. ﴿Controllers and subduers.﴾

﴿And We have subjected them to them﴾: made them subservient. ﴿Of them they have their riding animals﴾: the common reading is with fatha on the ra', meaning "their mount," as one says "a milch camel" (naqa halub), meaning "one that is milked." Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read it with damma on the ra' as a verbal noun.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hamdan related to us, saying: Ibn Hamman related to us, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama related to us, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwa, from ʿUrwa, who said: in the codex of ʿAʾisha it reads "rukubatuhum," and rakub and rakuba are the same, like hamul and hamula. ﴿And of them they eat﴾: their flesh.

﴿And for them in them are benefits﴾: from their wool, their flesh, and other benefits. ﴿And drinks﴾: that is, their milk. ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾

﴿And they have taken gods besides God, that they might be helped﴾: that is, to protect them from the punishment of God, and that will never happen.

﴿They cannot help them, and they are for them a host brought forward﴾ in the Fire, for they are with their idols in the Fire, and so none of them can repel the Fire from another.

﴿So let not their words grieve you﴾: that is, their denial, their harm and their hostility. The speech is complete here, and then He begins anew: ﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾

﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop, and then he is an open adversary, disputing falsely?﴾

They differed about who this man was. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he is ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he is al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. al-Hasan said: he is Umayya ibn Khalaf.

Qatada said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, for he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone that had crumbled, and said: "O Muhammad, do you think God will bring this to life after it has rotted?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and admit you into the Fire." [84] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 15/58.]]

So God revealed this verse: ﴿And he has presented to Us a parable and forgotten his own creation﴾, the beginning of his affair. ﴿He says: Who will give life to these bones when they are decayed?﴾ It is said "rimim" and not "rimima" because it is an adjective of the form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and whatever is diverted from its form and pattern is also diverted from its inflection, as in His saying: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾ [[Surat Maryam: 28.]], where the ta' marbuta is dropped because it is diverted from baghiya.

﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knower of every creation.﴾ ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾: it is not said "khadr" (green) but "akhdar" (greener) and "shajar" (trees, plural of shajara), because He returned it to the wording.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: there are two trees, one called markh and the other ʿaffar. Whoever among them wanted fire would cut two branches like siwak sticks, both green and dripping with water, and he would rub the markh, which is the male, against the ʿaffar, which is the female, and fire would come out of them by God's permission, the Mighty and Majestic.

The Arabs say: in every tree there is fire, and "istamjada al-markh wal-ʿaffar" (the markh and ʿaffar were rubbed for fire). The wise said: every tree has fire except the jujube (al-ʿinab). ﴿Then from it you kindle fire﴾: that is their provision.

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ The common reading is with alif; Ya'qub read "biqadir" as a verb. ﴿Yes, and He is the Creator, the Knowing.﴾ ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

﴿And We have subjected them to them﴾: made them subservient. ﴿Of them they have their riding animals﴾: the common reading is with fatha on the ra', meaning "their mount," as one says "a milch camel" (naqa halub), meaning "one that is milked." Al-A'mash and al-Hasan read it with damma on the ra' as a verbal noun.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hamdan related to us, saying: Ibn Hamman related to us, saying: Musa ibn Isma'il related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama related to us, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwa, from ʿUrwa, who said: in the codex of ʿAʾisha it reads "rukubatuhum," and rakub and rakuba are the same, like hamul and hamula. ﴿And of them they eat﴾: their flesh.

﴿And for them in them are benefits﴾: from their wool, their flesh, and other benefits. ﴿And drinks﴾: that is, their milk. ﴿Will they not then be thankful?﴾

﴿And they have taken gods besides God, that they might be helped﴾: that is, to protect them from the punishment of God, and that will never happen.

﴿They cannot help them, and they are for them a host brought forward﴾ in the Fire, for they are with their idols in the Fire, and so none of them can repel the Fire from another.

﴿So let not their words grieve you﴾: that is, their denial, their harm and their hostility. The speech is complete here, and then He begins anew: ﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾

﴿Has not man seen that We created him from a drop, and then he is an open adversary, disputing falsely?﴾

They differed about who this man was. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he is ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he is al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. al-Hasan said: he is Umayya ibn Khalaf.

Qatada said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, for he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone that had crumbled, and said: "O Muhammad, do you think God will bring this to life after it has rotted?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and admit you into the Fire." [84] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 15/58.]]

So God revealed this verse: ﴿And he has presented to Us a parable and forgotten his own creation﴾, the beginning of his affair. ﴿He says: Who will give life to these bones when they are decayed?﴾ It is said "rimim" and not "rimima" because it is an adjective of the form fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and whatever is diverted from its form and pattern is also diverted from its inflection, as in His saying: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾ [[Surat Maryam: 28.]], where the ta' marbuta is dropped because it is diverted from baghiya.

﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time, and He is Knower of every creation.﴾ ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾: it is not said "khadr" (green) but "akhdar" (greener) and "shajar" (trees, plural of shajara), because He returned it to the wording.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: there are two trees, one called markh and the other ʿaffar. Whoever among them wanted fire would cut two branches like siwak sticks, both green and dripping with water, and he would rub the markh, which is the male, against the ʿaffar, which is the female, and fire would come out of them by God's permission, the Mighty and Majestic.

The Arabs say: in every tree there is fire, and "istamjada al-markh wal-ʿaffar" (the markh and ʿaffar were rubbed for fire). The wise said: every tree has fire except the jujube (al-ʿinab). ﴿Then from it you kindle fire﴾: that is their provision.

﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾ The common reading is with alif; Ya'qub read "biqadir" as a verb. ﴿Yes, and He is the Creator, the Knowing.﴾ ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you will be returned.﴾
